ideas.title: Forge a hook at the kiln
ideas.critique: The glow cooling from yellow to red is the glass films again, and the island has had two hot-material close-ups in a row. What is strong is the elastoplastic solid: blows that stay as facets, hot versus cold response, and a hook that is then judged by whether it holds a load. But a GPU von Mises FEM with temperature-dependent yield is a big build, and if the bar only bends along a scripted curve the whole claim falls.

ideas.title: A basket that holds or spills
ideas.critique: A woven thing that is strong only because of friction and the pattern is really new for the island, and seeing berries leak through a gap you left is an honest, readable result. Discrete elastic rods with rod-rod frictional contact under load is research-grade, and threading over and under with a mouse is fiddly. The likeliest version is reeds on fixed paths with a gap test, and that is a look, not a weave.

ideas.title: The chisel bites the spinning log
ideas.critique: This is round 1's lathe with the missing mechanism added: a cutting force from depth and speed, torque that sags, and a catch that kicks back. Those are what make it a chisel and not a spline, and the top then spins by its own profile. Still, the tops post came just before, so it only surprises if the kickback and the slowing lathe are clearly felt and seen.

ideas.title: Clay that slumps on the wheel
ideas.critique: Clay that fails by its own water content and wall thickness puts the risk of collapse into the kick wheel, and that is the core of the goal. A shell of revolution, though, can only sag symmetrically. The folding-in and buckling the pitch promises are non-axisymmetric and will not come out of that model, so the film may show a pot that just squashes evenly.

ideas.title: Knots that hold
ideas.critique: A bowline that holds next to a granny that slips, both decided by capstan friction and self-contact, would be striking physics the island has never had. But rope self-contact that holds a knot without tunnelling is very hard, and tying knots with a mouse is a UI problem before it is physics. A knot also keeps its mark only until it is untied, so it sits at the edge of the workshop goal.

ideas.title: Wet sand keeps a print
ideas.nearest: A snowball that grows as it rolls, a take that misses
ideas.critique: This is round 1's cohesive sand turned toward the goal. Damp versus dry reads at a glance, and the GPU grains with cohesion that fades are real new physics. A footprint in sand is the most expected picture there is, though, and the casting that would give it a use is only promised, so for now it is something to press and look at.

ideas.title: A blade with nicks
ideas.nearest: Chipping a stone to change its note
same_form: Chipping a stone to change its note
ideas.critique: Wear is the real step past round 1's flint: every hard cut changes the edge, so the tool keeps its history, which is exactly what the goal is about. The knapping has already been filmed, though. The weak point is still the same: 'cutting force from the measured angle and radius' tends to end up as a sharpness number that switches between slice and tear, and then it is a threshold, not a cut.
